references.text: John the Baptist repeats his testimony that Jesus is the one who "comes after" him, yet has precedence over him ([ref:Joh 1:27|John 1:27]).
John repeats almost word for word the same declaration: "After me comes a man who was before me, because he existed before me" ([ref:Joh 1:30|John 1:30]).
The prologue of the Gospel of John introduces John as a witness sent from God to testify about the light, which aligns with his "testifying" (μαρτυρεῖ) here about Christ ([ref:Joh 1:6-8|John 1:6-8]).
The statement "he was before me" (πρῶτός μου ἦν) points back to the preexistence of the Word: "In the beginning was the Word" ([ref:Joh 1:1-2|John 1:1-2]).
John the Baptist again confirms that he is not the Messiah, but has been sent ahead for him, and that Jesus must increase while he himself must decrease ([ref:Joh 3:28-30|John 3:28-30]).
In the Gospel of Matthew, John the Baptist says that the one coming after him is stronger than he is, a parallel testimony to Jesus' superiority ([ref:Matt 3:11|Matthew 3:11]).
Mark records John the Baptist's preaching that one is coming after him who is stronger, and for whom he is not worthy to untie his sandal strap ([ref:Mark 1:7|Mark 1:7]).
Luke recounts the same testimony from John the Baptist about the one who is stronger and comes after him ([ref:Luk 3:16|Luke 3:16]).
Jesus' own words "Before Abraham was born, I am" confirm the preexistence that John the Baptist testifies to with "he was before me" ([ref:Joh 8:58|John 8:58]).
In his high priestly prayer, Jesus speaks of the glory he had with the Father before the world began, which supports the preexistence expressed in John 1:15 ([ref:Joh 17:5|John 17:5]).
Paul writes that Christ is before all things, and in him all things hold together – a parallel to "he was before me" ([ref:Kol 1:17|Colossians 1:17]).
The prophecy about the ruler from Bethlehem whose origin is from ancient times, from days of eternity, points to the preexistence that John the Baptist testifies to ([ref:Mi 5:1|Micah 5:1]).
